chunks: "I treat the sense resistor as a four-terminal device even if the part only has two pads.
The load current goes straight through the resistor's pads on wide copper, a pour or a short fat trace.
The measurement is made separately: two thin sense traces start at the inside edge of each pad, that is, right where the resistive element begins, and they go off to the amplifier.
That way the sense lines see only the drop across the resistor, not the drop across the power copper feeding it. Then I treat the sense lines like a small differential signal.
They run together as a tight pair, as short as possible, over a solid ground plane, away from the switch node, the inductor and any gate drive.
If I need an input filter I put the small RC right at the amplifier pins, and the amplifier right by the end of the pair.
The pair doesn't cross a plane split or run alongside a noisy trace.
Last thing, I connect the amplifier's ground to the resistor's ground side with a clean path, so the load return current isn't flowing through the reference I'm measuring against.
I'd also check power and temperature: P = I²R in the resistor, with enough copper to spread the heat."
